# Fenwick staff could see which instruments awaited parts

A six-week trial of a shared bench schedule gave Fenwick Instrument Repairs one place for jobs waiting on parts and jobs ready for work. Workshop manager Priya Vale explains what the team had to agree before the schedule was useful, and what Vale would do differently next time.

By Thomas

Fenwick Instrument Repairs services brass and woodwind instruments. In January 2026 its workshop team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule from Benchline, the scheduling software supplier publishing this account. Until then, jobs awaiting parts and jobs ready for work had appeared on separate paper sheets.

## The workshop set the rules and Benchline configured them

The team chose Benchline after checking that it could tell those two statuses apart. The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them. Benchline configured those choices and trained four staff in one online session, while collection arrangements were still discussed with customers by telephone.

Agreeing the definitions was the first task. Asked by email what the team had to settle before the schedule was useful, Vale replied: ‘We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench.’

## The summary counts jobs, not repair times

The workshop's own summary of the trial, dated 23 February 2026, says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts. It records 38 jobs entered in the schedule. It does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction.

Vale approved continued use for new jobs. Adding the backlog was postponed until the team had reviewed its status definitions.

## Fenwick's manager looks back on the trial

Asked whether the workshop would make the same choice again, and what would change, Vale wrote: ‘I would use it again for new jobs. I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog.’

Fenwick's experience is one team's report rather than a measured result. A manager weighing a shared schedule can still start where Fenwick's team did: by agreeing what each status means on their own benches.
EOF

# Source-support report: draft-2.md against source.md

Draft language: British English (en_GB). Source language: English. There is no translation, so this report has no translation findings. Quotations are in the source language and are checked for verbatim fidelity only.

## 1. Claim accounting

Each item gives the draft passage (D), the source passage (S) and what differs.

### Title
1. D: "Fenwick reports seeing which instruments awaited parts"
   S: "The workshop's trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, ... says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts."
   Difference: the draft names the source as "Fenwick" (the workshop) where the source names the workshop's trial summary. The summary is the workshop's own document, so the attribution holds. "could see" with a perception verb normally reports what was perceived, so "seeing" does not change the modality. Tense is carried correctly ("awaited"). No finding.

### Standfirst
2. D: "A six-week trial put jobs awaiting parts and jobs ready for work on one shared schedule at Fenwick Instrument Repairs."
   S: "began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule. Previously, jobs awaiting parts and jobs ready for work appeared on separate paper sheets. The team chose Benchline after checking that it could distinguish these statuses." Also: "records 38 jobs entered in the schedule".
   Difference: the source implies that both kinds of job now share one schedule ("Previously ... separate"), and the draft states it. The draft does not say that the trial finished. No finding.
3. D: "Manager Priya Vale explains what the team had to agree before it was useful, and what Vale would change."
   S: Question: "What did the team have to settle before the schedule was useful?" Vale: "We had to agree what ready for work meant." Question: "... what would you change?" Vale: "I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog."
   Difference: none of substance. "it" refers to the schedule (third person singular, not a person). Vale is referred to by name, so no gender is assigned. No finding.

### Byline
4. D: "By Thomas". This is excluded by instruction and is not a finding.

### Body, paragraph 1
5. D: "Fenwick Instrument Repairs services brass and woodwind instruments."
   S: "Fenwick Instrument Repairs services brass and woodwind instruments." The two are identical.
6. D: "In January 2026 its workshop team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule from Benchline, the scheduling software supplier publishing this account."
   S: "In January 2026 the workshop team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule." "The team chose Benchline". Brief: "The publisher is scheduling software supplier Benchline".
   Difference: none. "its" refers to Fenwick (third person singular, not a person). No finding.
7. D: "Before then, jobs awaiting parts and jobs ready for work appeared on separate paper sheets."
   S: "Previously, jobs awaiting parts and jobs ready for work appeared on separate paper sheets."
   Difference: "Before then" pins the time to before the trial. In context, the source's "Previously" means the same. No finding.

### Heading: "The workshop set the rules and Benchline configured them"
8. S: "The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them. Benchline configured those choices".
   Difference: "the rules" is a heading summary of the status definitions and the update responsibilities. "them" is third person plural and refers to the rules. The division of roles is preserved. No finding.

### Body, section 1
9. D: "The team chose Benchline after checking that it could tell those two statuses apart."
   S: "The team chose Benchline after checking that it could distinguish these statuses."
   Difference: "tell ... apart" is a synonym for "distinguish", and the sequence is preserved. "it" is Benchline. No finding.
10. D: "The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them; Benchline configured those choices and trained four staff in one online session."
    S: The same wording across two sentences. The figure (four) and the manner (one online session) match. No finding.
11. D: "Collection arrangements were still discussed with customers by telephone."
    S: "The team continued to use telephone calls to discuss collection arrangements with customers."
    Difference: the draft uses the passive and leaves out the agent. "still" carries "continued". The draft claims neither exclusivity nor anything beyond what the source says. No finding.
12. D: "Asked by email what the team had to settle before the schedule was useful, workshop manager Priya Vale wrote: 'We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench.'"
    S: "email interview on 2 March 2026 between Benchline's case writer and workshop manager Priya Vale" and Question: "What did the team have to settle before the schedule was useful?" Vale: "We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench."
    Difference: the medium (email, "wrote") is correct. The quotation is verbatim apart from British single quotation marks. "We" is Vale's own first-person plural (the team). No finding.

### Heading: "The summary counts jobs, not repair times"
13. S: "records 38 jobs entered in the schedule. ... It does not measure repair duration".
    Difference: none of substance. No finding.

### Body, section 2
14. D: "The workshop's own trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts."
    S: The same wording. No finding.
15. D: "It records 38 jobs entered in the schedule."
    S: The same wording. The figure is exact. No finding.
16. D: "It does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction."
    S: The same wording. No finding.

### Heading: "Fenwick's manager settles the next step"
17. S: "The manager approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions."
    Difference: "settles" means decides. The decision includes the postponement, which the body carries. No finding.

### Body, section 3
18. D: "Vale approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions."
    S: "The manager approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions."
    Difference: the draft identifies "the manager" as Vale. The source's only named manager is "workshop manager Priya Vale". The brief refers to "its manager" in the singular. The interview question "Would you make the same choice again" is put to Vale as the person who made the choice. The identification is therefore supported. The condition ("until ... reviewed") is preserved. "its" refers to the team. No finding.
19. D: "Would Vale make the same choice again, and change anything? 'I would use it again for new jobs. I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog.'"
    S: Question: "Would you make the same choice again, and what would you change?" Vale: "I would use it again for new jobs. I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog."
    Difference: the question is paraphrased in the third person. "change anything" is a yes/no question where the source asks "what would you change", which is a question to the interviewee and not a claim. The answer is verbatim. The source does not say what "the same choice" refers to. Because the draft places it right after the approval sentence, a reader may take it to mean the approval decision. Vale's answer ("use it again for new jobs") and her backlog remark fit either reading, and the draft keeps the source's own words, so no concrete case separates the two. No finding. This is noted only as an editorial observation.

### Closing paragraph
20. D: "This is one team's reported experience, not a measured result."
    S: "The summary and interview establish the team's reported experience, not a measured improvement in repair speed or a recommendation for every workshop." Also: "records 38 jobs entered in the schedule. ... It does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction."
    Difference: the source's scope is narrow ("a measured improvement in repair speed"). The draft widens it to any "measured result". See Finding 1.
21. D: "A manager weighing a shared schedule might begin with what Fenwick had to settle: agreeing what each status means at their own benches."
    S: Vale: "We had to agree what ready for work meant." "The workshop defined the statuses".
    Difference: this is the author's advice to readers, resting on supported material. It is not a recommendation that every workshop adopt the schedule, so it does not contradict the source's "not ... a recommendation for every workshop". "each status" is supported by the workshop defining the statuses. "their" is the generic singular they for "a manager" and carries no gender. No finding.

## 2. Pronoun accounting (person, number, natural gender)
- "its" (paragraph 1): third person singular, not a person (Fenwick). Supported.
- "it" (standfirst, section 1): third person singular, not a person (the schedule; Benchline). Supported.
- "them" (heading, section 1): third person plural, not a person (rules; statuses). Supported.
- "We" and "I" (inside quotations): the speaker's own first person, singular and plural, as in the source. Unchanged.
- "its" (section 3): third person singular, not a person (the team). Supported.
- "their" (closing): generic singular they for "a manager". It asserts no natural gender.
- Priya Vale is referred to only by name throughout. The draft asserts no natural gender, and the source records none. English has no grammatical gender here.

## 3. Findings (source support)

### Finding 1: the closing paragraph widens the source's "not a measured improvement in repair speed" to "not a measured result"
- Draft: "This is one team's reported experience, not a measured result."
- Source: "The summary and interview establish the team's reported experience, not a measured improvement in repair speed or a recommendation for every workshop."
- What changed: scope. The source rules out a measured improvement in repair speed, and says the summary does not measure duration, revenue or satisfaction. It does not say that the trial produced nothing measured. The draft denies any measured result.
- Concrete case: the trial summary records a counted figure, "38 jobs entered in the schedule". That is a quantified trial outcome, so the draft's statement fails while the source's statement holds. No supplied statement rules this case out.
- Smallest supported repair: "This is one team's reported experience, not a measured improvement in repair speed."

## 4. Translation findings
None. Source and draft are both in English, and all quotations are reproduced verbatim.

## 5. Completion status
Complete. Every factual and attributed claim in the title, standfirst, headings, body and closing has been accounted for. One source-support finding is unresolved: Finding 1, the closing sentence's widened scope. There are no translation findings.
